promptText: Why does React favor composition over inheritance for sharing behavior between components?
options: Composition couples components only to a public prop contract, avoiding the fragile base-class problem inheritance introduces, and composes without a single-parent limit
JavaScript does not support class inheritance at all
Inheritance is disallowed by the JSX compiler
Composition is faster at runtime because it avoids virtual DOM diffing
explanation: The React team has stated they never found a case where inheritance across components beat composition; coupling only to a prop contract is far easier to reason about and refactor than a class hierarchy.

promptText: Why has the strict container/presentational component split become less emphasized since hooks were introduced?
options: Hooks let you extract stateful logic into a function without needing a dedicated wrapper component just to hold that state
Container components are no longer supported by React's reconciler
Presentational components can no longer accept props
React deprecated class components, which the pattern required
explanation: The pattern existed because class components had no way to reuse stateful logic without a wrapper; a custom hook now plays the old container's role without adding an extra component.

promptText: Why does a ref attached to a component wrapped by a hand-written HOC (that just spreads {...props}) end up null?
options: ref is not a regular prop — it's never included in a spread of props, so it silently fails to reach the underlying component unless the HOC explicitly uses forwardRef
HOCs cannot render any component that accepts a ref
Refs only work on class components, never on function components wrapped in HOCs
The ref is actually forwarded correctly; the described bug does not occur
explanation: React special-cases ref so it never appears inside props, meaning a naive spread-based HOC drops it entirely; forwardRef exists specifically to plug this hole.

promptText: In render-prop libraries like react-window, why can't a plain custom hook replace the render-prop entirely?
options: A hook can only return data; it cannot control where or whether something renders in the tree, but the library needs to decide exactly which rows exist in the DOM and where
Hooks cannot be called inside virtualization libraries for technical reasons
Render props are strictly faster than any hook-based alternative
TypeScript cannot type a hook that returns row data
explanation: Hooks share stateful logic, but virtualization requires the library itself to control layout and positioning of rendered content — something only a render prop or component-driven API can express.

promptText: In a compound component like <Tabs><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs>, why is Context preferred today over the older React.cloneElement plus React.Children.map approach?
options: Context flows to any depth in the tree regardless of intervening wrappers, while cloneElement only reaches direct children and silently breaks if a child is wrapped in another element
cloneElement was removed from React and no longer exists
Context is the only way to pass any prop to a child component
cloneElement requires all children to be class components
explanation: cloneElement-based prop injection stops working the moment a consumer wraps a child in a div or maps over an array, whereas Context ignores tree depth and structural changes entirely.

promptText: In the 'control props' pattern for a custom <Toggle value defaultValue onChange> component, how does the component decide whether it's controlled or uncontrolled?
options: By checking whether the value prop is undefined; if defined, it defers to that value on every render, otherwise it manages its own internal state
By checking which prop was passed first at the JSX call site during compilation
It is controlled only if defaultValue is omitted entirely
By comparing value and defaultValue for strict equality
explanation: The isControlled check is always value !== undefined, mirroring how React's own inputs decide between controlled and uncontrolled behavior.

promptText: Why does memoizing a Context provider's value with useMemo sometimes fail to prevent unnecessary consumer re-renders even when done correctly?
options: Context re-renders are all-or-nothing per provider with no field-level selector, so even a legitimately changed value re-renders every consumer regardless of which specific field it actually reads
useMemo does not work at all inside a Context.Provider's value prop
Context providers ignore memoized values and always trigger a re-render on every parent render
Memoization only works for primitive values, not objects
explanation: Memoizing the value fixes the 'new reference every render' problem, but a genuine change to one field still re-renders every consumer since Context has no way to subscribe to just part of a value.

promptText: What is the most commonly cited limitation of error boundaries?
options: They do not catch errors thrown inside event handlers or asynchronous code such as setTimeout or promises, only errors during rendering or lifecycle methods
They can only be used once per application
They must be written as function components using hooks
They can only catch errors from third-party libraries, not your own code
explanation: Error boundaries rely on the render/commit error-handling pathway; anything thrown outside that path (an event handler, an async callback) needs an ordinary try/catch instead.

promptText: Mechanically, how does <Suspense> know when to show its fallback?
options: A suspending component throws a promise; the nearest Suspense boundary catches it, renders the fallback, and re-renders children once the promise resolves
Suspense polls a global isLoading flag on every render
It relies on a special loading prop that every component must implement
It inspects network requests directly via the browser's Performance API
explanation: Suspense works like an error boundary but catches thrown promises instead of thrown errors, showing the fallback until the caught promise resolves.

promptText: A modal rendered via ReactDOM.createPortal into document.body has a click handler on an ancestor React component. Does clicking inside the modal trigger that ancestor's click handler, and why?
options: Yes — event bubbling in React follows the React component tree, not the DOM tree, so the event still bubbles up through the ancestor that logically rendered the portal
No — portaled content is completely isolated from the rest of the React event system
Only if the portal target is inside the same DOM subtree as the ancestor
It depends on whether the ancestor uses onClick versus onClickCapture; otherwise it never bubbles
explanation: Portals move DOM output but not logical tree position; React's synthetic event bubbling still follows where the component was rendered in the React tree, which surprises people expecting DOM-based bubbling.

promptText: After a production deploy, some users see a React.lazy chunk-load failure for a route they haven't yet visited. What's the root cause and the standard mitigation?
options: Their browser is requesting an old, now-deleted hashed chunk filename from before the deploy; wrap lazy routes in an error boundary that offers a reload or refetch
React.lazy is fundamentally incompatible with production builds and should only be used in development
The component was not wrapped in useMemo, causing the import to run twice
Suspense boundaries expire automatically after a fixed timeout in production
explanation: A stale client referencing an old hashed chunk after a new deploy is a well-known lazy-loading pitfall; pairing lazy routes with an error boundary that prompts a reload is the standard fix.

promptText: A modal's open/closed boolean is stored in a global Redux/Zustand store even though only one component ever reads or writes it. What's the recommended fix per the state-colocation principle?
options: Move it into local component state since a global store adds unnecessary re-render scope and coupling for state used by only one component
Duplicate the boolean into both the global store and local state to be safe
Convert it into a URL query parameter regardless of whether it needs to be shareable
Nothing — global state is always preferable for consistency across the codebase
explanation: State should be pushed down to the smallest scope that needs it; a single-component modal flag globalized for no reason adds re-render blast radius and test-setup overhead with zero benefit.

promptText: In a polymorphic <Button as={...}> component typed with React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>, what problem does this generic typing solve compared to typing 'as' as React.ElementType with untyped rest props?
options: It makes TypeScript infer the correct, tag-specific attribute set (e.g. href for 'a', onClick/disabled for 'button') based on whatever the as prop is set to at each call site, catching invalid props at compile time
It removes the need to ever pass an as prop at all
It makes the component render faster at runtime
It automatically generates unit tests for every possible as value
explanation: Making the component generic over the element type and intersecting with ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C> lets TypeScript re-infer the correct prop shape per call site instead of falling back to any/string.

promptText: What is the key mechanical difference between the 'as' prop pattern (styled-components, Chakra) and Radix's 'asChild' pattern?
options: 'as' swaps which tag or component the component itself renders; 'asChild' instead merges the component's behavior and props onto a single child element the consumer provides, without rendering an extra wrapper of its own
They are functionally identical, just named differently by different libraries
'asChild' only works with native HTML tags, never custom components
'as' requires a class component while 'asChild' requires a function component
explanation: asChild avoids the 'does my custom component accept the same props as a native tag' problem entirely by merging behavior onto the consumer's own element via a Slot mechanism, rather than swapping a tag name.

promptText: In a headless combobox implementation, why is aria-activedescendant often preferred over moving actual DOM focus to each highlighted option?
options: It lets the text input keep real DOM focus so typing keeps working normally, while still telling assistive technology which option is 'virtually' focused or highlighted
aria-activedescendant is required by the HTML spec for any list of more than five items
Moving real DOM focus is impossible on li elements in all browsers
It removes the need for any keyboard event handling in the component
explanation: A naive implementation that moves real focus to each option breaks typing and normal input behavior; aria-activedescendant keeps focus on the input while announcing the highlighted option to screen readers.
